q.t: What comes next? 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …
q.e: Even numbers go up by 2 each time.

q.t: What comes next in the odd numbers? 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …
q.e: Odd numbers start at 1 and go up by 2.

q.t: What is the next square number after 1, 4, 9, 16, 25?
q.e: Squares are 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, … The 6th is 6 × 6 = 36.

q.t: What is the next triangular number? 1, 3, 6, 10, …
q.e: Each triangle adds a new row one dot longer: +2, +3, +4, then +5. 10 + 5 = 15.

q.t: What is the next cube? 1, 8, 27, 64, …
q.e: Cubes are n × n × n. The 5th is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

q.t: What is the next power of 2? 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …
q.e: Powers of 2 double each time: 16 × 2 = 32.

q.t: What is the next Virahānka number? 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …
q.e: Each Virahānka number is the sum of the previous two: 5 + 8 = 13.

q.t: Mathematics is, in large part, the search for …
o: patterns, and the explanations of why they exist
the answers at the back of the book
q.e: The book's big idea: find the pattern, then explain why it happens — the explanation is what you can reuse.

q.t: Patterns in whole numbers are studied by which branch of maths?
q.e: Number theory studies patterns in whole numbers; geometry studies patterns in shapes.

q.t: How many sides does a regular hexagon have?
q.e: Hexa means six. The regular polygon sequence counts sides 3, 4, 5, 6, …

q.t: Find 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 without adding one by one.
q.e: These are the first 6 odd numbers. The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n, so 6 × 6 = 36.

q.t: What is the sum of the first 10 odd numbers?
q.e: The first n odd numbers add to n × n (they make L-shaped layers of a square). 10 × 10 = 100.
Adding up and down to 5 counts the diagonals of a 5 × 5 square, so the total is 5 × 5 = 25.

q.t: Add the consecutive triangular numbers 10 and 15. What kind of number do you get?
q.e: Two neighbouring triangles of dots fit together into a square: 10 + 15 = 25 = 5 × 5.

q.t: What is the next hexagonal number? 1, 7, 19, 37, …
q.e: Hexagonal numbers = triangular × 6 + 1. The 5th triangular number is 10, so 10 × 6 + 1 = 61.

q.t: How many lines are there in a complete graph with 4 dots (every dot joined to every other)?
q.e: The 2nd dot adds 1 line, the 3rd adds 2, the 4th adds 3: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, a triangular number.

q.t: Which number is both a triangular number and a square number?
q.e: 36 = 6 × 6, and 36 = 1 + 2 + … + 8, so its dots make both a square and a triangle.
Adding powers of 2 from 1 always gives one less than the next power of 2: 32 − 1 = 31.

q.t: A regular polygon must have …
o: all sides equal and all angles equal
q.e: Regular means both: equal sides and equal angles. A rhombus has equal sides but is not regular unless its angles are equal too.

q.t: How many line segments does the 2nd shape of the Koch snowflake have (the first is a triangle with 3)?
q.e: Every segment is replaced by a speed bump of 4 segments, so 3 × 4 = 12.

q.t: Find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 19 (all the odd numbers up to 19).
q.e: There are (19 + 1) ÷ 2 = 10 odd numbers up to 19, so the sum is 10 × 10 = 100. Count the numbers — don't use the last one.
Up and down to 100 counts the diagonals of a 100 × 100 square: 100 × 100 = 10,000.
Pair the ends: (1+10) + (2+9) + … + (5+6) = 5 pairs of 11 = 55. It is the 10th triangular number.

q.t: What is the 9th Virahānka number? 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …
q.e: Keep adding the previous two: 13 + 21 = 34 (8th), then 21 + 34 = 55 (9th).
The next power of 2 after 64 is 128; the sum is always one less: 128 − 1 = 127. (Add 1 and it snowballs: 1+1 = 2, 2+2 = 4, …, 64+64 = 128.)

q.t: Find 1 + 7 + 19 + 37 (adding hexagonal numbers).
q.e: Adding hexagonal numbers gives cubes, because each hexagon is one layer of a cube seen from its corner. 1 + 7 + 19 + 37 = 64 = 4 × 4 × 4.

q.t: Why does a regular polygon have as many corners as sides?
o: Every side ends at a corner where the next side begins
Because all its sides are equal
It doesn't — it has one more corner than sides
q.e: Walking round the shape you meet one corner after each side, then arrive back at the start — so the counts match for every closed polygon, regular or not.

q.t: How many lines are there in a complete graph with 6 dots?
q.e: Each new dot joins every dot already there: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.

q.t: A stacked-triangle shape has 4 rows. How many little triangles does it have?
q.e: The rows hold 1, 3, 5, 7 little triangles — the odd numbers — and 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4 × 4.

q.t: How many segments does the 4th Koch snowflake shape have (3, 12, 48, …)?
q.e: Each step every segment becomes 4: 48 × 4 = 192. The sequence is 3 × powers of 4.

q.t: Find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 199 (all odd numbers up to 199).
q.e: There are (199 + 1) ÷ 2 = 100 odd numbers, so the sum is 100 × 100 = 10,000.

q.t: 1 + 3 + 5 + … adds up to 144. How many odd numbers were added?
q.e: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n, and 12 × 12 = 144, so n = 12. (The last one added is 23.)

q.t: What is the 6th hexagonal number (1, 7, 19, 37, 61, …)?
q.e: Hexagonal = 6 × triangular + 1. The 6th triangular number is 15, so 15 × 6 + 1 = 91. (Check the jumps: +6, +12, +18, +24, +30.)

q.t: Which sequence do you get by multiplying each triangular number by 6 and adding 1, and why?
o: Hexagonal numbers — a hexagon is a centre dot with six triangles around it
Square numbers — two triangles make a square
q.e: Six equal triangles of dots around one centre dot make a hexagon: 6 × triangle + 1.

q.t: Find 1 + 7 + 19 + 37 + 61 (the first five hexagonal numbers).
q.e: Adding hexagonal numbers gives cubes. Five of them make 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.

q.t: If 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = N, what is N?
q.e: The next power of 2 after 512 is 1024, and the sum is one less: 1023.

q.t: A complete graph has 10 lines. How many dots does it have?
q.e: Lines go 1, 3, 6, 10 for 2, 3, 4, 5 dots (adding 1, 2, 3, 4). So 10 lines means 5 dots.

q.t: How many segments does the 5th Koch snowflake shape have?
q.e: 3, 12, 48, 192, 768 — multiply by 4 each step because each segment becomes 4.

q.t: Which of these is NOT a square number?
q.e: 49 = 7×7, 64 = 8×8, 81 = 9×9. 7×7 = 49 and 8×8 = 64, so 50 sits between squares and is not one.

q.t: The 10th triangular number and the 11th triangular number are added. What is the total?
q.e: 10th = 55, 11th = 66. Two consecutive triangular numbers make a square: 55 + 66 = 121 = 11 × 11.
